task_row_model.query: Let A be a compact, self-adjoint operator on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space H. Prove that H admits an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A, that the eigenvalues are real and accumulate only at 0, and outline how the Rayleigh quotient or variational (minimax) characterization is used to obtain the sequence of eigenvalues tending to zero.

documents.content: For a bounded self-adjoint operator T on a Hilbert space, the spectral theorem gives a projection-valued measure E on the Borel sets of the real line so that T = ∫ λ dE(λ). This decomposition yields a functional calculus and shows that the spectrum σ(T) is real and can include continuous parts: point, continuous and residual spectra. In general there need not be a countable orthonormal eigenbasis; continuous spectrum components prevent such a basis. The spectral measure approach is central to functional calculus but does not by itself guarantee discrete eigenvalues or accumulation behavior absent compactness assumptions.

The bounded inverse theorem in Banach spaces states that a bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces has a bounded inverse. For a bounded operator B on a Banach space, invertibility is equivalent to 0 not belonging to the spectrum σ(B). This criterion is useful for Fredholm theory and perturbation arguments: if B is invertible and K is compact with small norm, then B+K may remain Fredholm. These results regulate solvability of linear equations and stability under compact perturbations, but they do not by themselves produce an orthonormal eigenbasis or control accumulation of eigenvalues for compact self-adjoint operators.

If A is compact and self-adjoint on a separable Hilbert space H, then every nonzero point λ in the spectrum is an eigenvalue of finite multiplicity, eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal, and there exists an orthonormal basis of H consisting of eigenvectors of A together with possibly the zero vector if 0 is in the spectrum. A standard proof uses the variational characterization: define the Rayleigh quotient R(x)=⟨Ax,x⟩/⟨x,x⟩ and choose a unit vector maximizing R on the orthogonal complement of previously found eigenvectors to obtain a sequence of eigenvalues λ1≥λ2≥⋯. Compactness ensures no accumulation except at 0, so λn→0 and the eigenspaces span H.

Compact operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces share key spectral properties: the spectrum is countable with possible accumulation only at 0, and every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue of finite algebraic multiplicity. One can approximate a compact operator by finite-rank operators in operator norm; spectral information of the approximants produces the discrete eigenvalues of the compact operator. For normal compact operators (including self-adjoint ones) one obtains a discrete orthonormal set of eigenvectors spanning the closure of the range, but some expositions stop short of the complete orthonormal basis statement unless self-adjointness or normality is explicitly invoked.

Unbounded self-adjoint operators such as differential operators on noncompact domains often have continuous spectrum and generalized eigenfunctions rather than a discrete set of eigenvalues. For example, the Laplacian on R^n has spectrum [0,∞) with no orthonormal basis of square-integrable eigenfunctions; solutions are expressed via Fourier transform and spectral measures. Deficiency indices and self-adjoint extensions govern domain issues for unbounded operators. These features contrast with compact operators, since compactness forces discreteness of nonzero spectrum and precludes extended continuous spectral bands familiar from differential operators on noncompact manifolds.
